newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY'S RUN-HIT POSTABANK SEEKS FOREIGN OWNERS.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY'S RUN-HIT POSTABANK SEEKS FOREIGN OWNERS.

text.p: Postabank, Hungary's second largest commercial bank said on Friday it planned to pursue its efforts to attract foreign investors to improve their credit ratings and competitiveness.

Postabank officials told a news conference that a recent 25 billion forint five-day run of withdrawals by depositors scared by rumours about the bank's solvency problems could not ruin Postabank's market position.
The run ended on Monday after assurances by Hungary's government and banking authorities and by Moody's that the bank was sound soothed investors.

Postabank CEO and chairman Gabor Princz said the bank was continuing its search for strategic investors which could acquire a 15 to 40 percent stake in the bank in a capital increase planned for this year.
"Our bank, which has become the second largest in Hungary in nine year of continuous effort, raises its capital almost every second year," Princz said. "We need to because of our rapid expansion."
Princz confirmed earlier reports that the bank appointed SBC Warburg to search for foreign investors which would acquire a stake in the bank.
Warburg said in a statement earlier on Friday that Postabank's plan was part of a long standing strategy to reinforce its shareholder base.
Princz added that following nine years of expansion of assets, Postabank would like devote more attention to improving its profitability, as suggested by the State Banking Supervision last year.

Postabank earlier said it had boosted its assets by more than 40 percent last year, while according to preliminary figures the bank's pre-tax profit rose to 3.17 billion forints in 1996 from 2.83 billion in 1995.

Janos Lakatos, chairman and CEO of the bank's borkerage, Postabank Securities said Postabank needed a foreign strategic investor as the increasing penetration of foreign banks into the Hungarian financial sector boosted competition.

"Due to the privatisation, the bank sector around us has changed and we have to strengthen our foreign relations to improve our credit rating," he said. "Otherwise the country's rating would be the highest we could get."
The National Bank of Hungary is rated BBB minus by Standard and Poor and Baa3 by Moody's.

Foreign giants like the Netherlands ING and ABN-Amro and the U.S.'s General Electric Capital Services already hold strong positions in Hungary's retail banking and plan to increase their market share.
Hungary also plans this year to sell K&H, the last large bank still to be privatised.
Princz said the current owners of Postabank may also boost their stakes in the bank

Some 35 percent of the registered capital is held by Hungary's social security funds. Oesterreischische Postsparkasse holds 10.4 percent while the stake of Bank Austria was about three percent, Lakatos said.
